note_sections.t: Routine follow-up consultation regarding previously diagnosed low-volume prostate adenocarcinoma to discuss long-term management options.

A 55-year-old primary school teacher attends this clinic for routine surveillance following his initial prostate biopsy. He reports a stable urinary stream with a self-scored IPSS of 11, noting mild hesitancy but no nocturia or urgency. His general medical history is unremarkable, with no current medications and no known drug allergies. He remains an ex-smoker, having ceased a 27 pack-year habit in 2009, and maintains an active lifestyle with approximately 30 kilometers of cycling three times weekly alongside moderate alcohol consumption. Socially, he is married and resides with his partner, with his brother serving as his primary contact. Recent routine podiatric care for mild plantar fasciitis has been managed conservatively, and he has requested future clinic visits be scheduled in the morning to accommodate his public transit commute.

Per rectum, the prostate gland measures approximately 57 mL with a smooth, symmetrical contour and no palpable nodules or asymmetry, correlating with a clinical stage of cT1c. General examination is unremarkable, with stable vital signs including a blood pressure of 121/78 mmHg and a heart rate of 78 bpm, alongside a lean body habitus with a BMI of 19.0.
